name: Inception
blurb: Nolan's heist film about a team that plants an idea deep inside a man's dreams
title: Inception Explained: Plot Summary and Ending
description: Inception explained: the team, the dream levels, kicks, limbo and totems, the full plot of the Fischer job, and what the spinning top at the end means.
h1: Inception Explained: Plot, Dream Levels and Ending
answer: Inception is a 2010 science-fiction heist film written and directed by Christopher Nolan, starring Leonardo DiCaprio. Dom Cobb is a thief who uses military-designed technology to enter people's dreams and steal secrets from their subconscious. A powerful businessman offers him a way home to his children, whom he has not seen since he fled the United States, if he can do the reverse: plant an idea in a rival's mind so deeply that the man believes it is his own. The film follows the job through dreams nested inside dreams, while Cobb is haunted by his late wife.

body.note: Key terms. Levels: a dream inside a dream; time runs slower the deeper you go. Kick: a jolt, such as a fall, that wakes a dreamer. Limbo: raw, endless subconscious where a dreamer can be lost for what feels like decades. Totem: a small personal object whose weight or behaviour only its owner knows, used to tell a dream from reality; Cobb's is a spinning top that, in a dream, never falls.

body: Beginning. Cobb and Arthur try to steal secrets from Saito's mind using a dream within a dream, but Saito sees through it. He was testing them. He offers Cobb a job: inception, planting an idea rather than stealing one. The target is Robert Fischer, whose father Maurice is dying and will leave him a giant energy company that Saito wants broken up. In return Saito will use his influence to clear the murder charge that keeps Cobb from going home to his two children in Los Angeles. In Paris, Cobb recruits Ariadne as architect, and in Mombasa he finds Eames and Yusuf. Ariadne discovers that Cobb's subconscious is dangerous: a projection of his wife Mal keeps sabotaging his jobs.

Middle. When Maurice dies, Robert takes the ten-hour flight from Sydney to Los Angeles with his father's body. The team drugs him and enters a three-level dream. Level one is a rainy city dreamed by Yusuf, where armed projections from Robert's trained subconscious attack them and Saito is badly wounded. Cobb reveals that Yusuf's heavy sedation means anyone who dies now will not wake up but fall into limbo. Eames poses as Browning to suggest that Maurice left a secret will. Cobb then tells Ariadne about Mal. Years earlier, he and Mal built a world together in limbo and lived there for what felt like fifty years. To make her leave, Cobb planted in her mind the idea that her world was not real. Back in reality the idea stayed with her: she became convinced she was still dreaming, and she killed herself after arranging things so that Cobb would be blamed, hoping he would follow her. He fled the country.

Level two is a hotel dreamed by Arthur. Cobb persuades Robert that he is a protector and that Browning is behind the kidnapping, and leads him down to level three, a snowy mountain fortress dreamed by Eames, where a vault will hold the idea. On level one Yusuf's van goes off a bridge too early, which makes gravity vanish in the hotel, so Arthur has to improvise a kick for his sleeping team. On level three, Mal appears and shoots Robert, and Saito dies of his wounds. Cobb and Ariadne go down into limbo, where Cobb confronts Mal in the ruins of the world they built. He admits his guilt and finally lets her go, and Ariadne sends Robert back up. Robert reaches the vault and finds his dying father, who tells him he was disappointed that Robert tried to be like him. Robert accepts the planted idea: to build something of his own and break up the empire.

What happens: Cobb stays in limbo to look for Saito. He finds him as a very old man, which is the scene that opened the film, and reminds him of their deal. Everyone wakes on the plane. Saito picks up a phone and makes a call, and Cobb walks through immigration at Los Angeles with no problem. Miles takes him home. Cobb spins his top on a table, then walks out to the garden to see his children's faces for the first time in the film. The camera moves back to the top. It spins, seems to wobble slightly, and the film cuts to black before it falls or keeps going.
Whether the final scene is real or a dream is the most debated question about the film. The main positions:

ol: It is real. The top seems to wobble at the very end, and Michael Caine has said Nolan told him that scenes with his character are reality while scenes without him are dreams, and Caine is in the final scene.
It is still a dream. Cobb never wakes from limbo, or the whole film is his dream; the top is not even his original totem but Mal's, so it cannot prove anything to him.

It does not matter. This is the reading Nolan himself has given. He has said the cut was his deliberate choice to impose ambiguity, that the real point is that Cobb is no longer watching the top but looking at his children, and in 2023 he credited producer Emma Thomas with the right answer: Cobb does not care at that point.

body: Nolan has never said whether the top falls. What the film settles is emotional: Cobb has let go of Mal and of his need to check, and he has chosen the life in front of him.

ul: Guilt: Cobb's projection of Mal is his own guilt for planting the idea that destroyed her, and the job is also his therapy.
Reality and illusion: the film keeps asking how anyone knows they are awake, and whether it matters if a life feels real.
The power of ideas: Cobb treats an idea as something almost impossible to remove once planted; one planted in Mal killed her, one planted in Robert frees him.
Fathers and children: Robert's need for his father's approval and Cobb's longing for his children drive both main stories.
Filmmaking: many critics read the team as a film crew, with a director, a designer, an actor and a producer building a world for an audience.
Runtime: 148 minutes. English-language, released in July 2010.
An original screenplay by Nolan, not an adaptation; his producer and wife Emma Thomas produced it with him.
Content: rated PG-13 in the US; there is a lot of gunfire but little blood, and a suicide that is discussed and briefly shown.
Tip for first-time viewers: keep track of which dream level each scene is on; the last hour cuts between four levels at once, each running at a different speed.

options: Stealing a secret from a dream
Planting an idea so the target thinks it is his own
check.why: Saito asks Cobb to plant, not steal, an idea in Robert Fischer's mind.

check.q: Why can't Cobb go home to the United States?
options: He is accused of killing his wife, Mal
He owes money to the dream-technology company
check.why: Mal staged her suicide so Cobb would be blamed, and he fled the country to avoid the charge.

check.q: What idea does the team plant in Robert Fischer?
options: That he should sell the company to Saito
That his father wanted him to be his own man and break up the empire
check.why: In the vault his dying father tells him he wanted Robert to stop trying to be like him.

faq.q: Does the top fall at the end of Inception?
faq.a: The film cuts to black while it is still spinning, just after a slight wobble. Nolan has never answered the question and has said the point is that Cobb no longer cares.

faq.q: Was Mal right that Cobb was still dreaming?
faq.a: Some viewers think so, but the film presents her belief as the result of the idea Cobb planted in limbo, and Cobb's guilt over it is the core of his story.

faq.q: How many dream levels are there in Inception?
faq.a: The Fischer job uses three levels, a rainy city, a hotel and a snowy fortress, plus limbo below them, where Cobb, Ariadne, Robert and Saito end up.
